thread.title: Netflix: 3 Reasons You Should Be Worried About This Stock - Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX) | Seeking Alpha

author: Robert Riesen
title: Netflix: 3 Reasons You Should Be Worried About This Stock - Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX) | Seeking Alpha
text:
There's few hotter stocks on the market right now than Netflix ( NFLX ). Over the last year, the price has increased approximately 115%. With that being said, I believe the stock is way over-bought and really setting up for a correction in the near-term for the following reasons:
Much of Netflix's stock performance has been a result of increasing valuation multiples and less so on actual performance improvement. Pay particular attention to Netflix's Price/Sales multiple, which trades at the same level of Facebook ( FB ) and nearly twice the level of Google ( GOOG ). To finance its content production costs, Netflix has turned to the debt markets. Increasing leverage before producing positive free cash flow is risky. Netflix's free cash flow projections are actually downright scary at the moment. A few years ago Netflix was the clear low-cost alternative to cable television. This just isn't the case anymore and chord-cutters have an increasing amount of choice in the $8 - $20 per month range. In my opinion, this will reduce Netflix's ability to increase its prices in the future without increasing customer churn. Netflix's Financial Snapshot Netflix's performance has mostly been impressive with strong revenue and subscriber growth. What I don't like is negative free cash flow production from content production costs (most of which get logged into ''content assets'' on its balance sheet). This is projected to be in the negative $3 - $4 billion range during 2018 and Moody's doesn't expect positive free cash flow production until 2022.
Data Source: Netflix's SEC Filings 1. Valuation at Unsustainable Levels Historical Price/Sales Multiple
The chart below probably gives me the most concern. Netflix's current Price/Sales multiple is well above its historical average and basically at an all-time high. Netflix's Price/Sales wasn't even this high after its IPO. Keep in mind that the content creation business is low margin and other content creators generally trade below a 4x multiple. Most high margin and high cash flow tech companies don't even trade at such a high multiple.
NFLX data by YCharts
Valuation Per Subscriber
As you'll see in the table below, each Netflix subscriber is valued at $1,253, yet that customer only brings in an average of $118 per year. Since 2016, this valuation has basically doubled. Revenue per customer has improved given membership prices increases, but this shouldn't have equaled such a drastic subscriber valuation increase.
Comparative Analysis
Netflix looks overvalued whether compared to other content providers or fast growing online technology companies. The Price/Sales ratio and gross margins are what's most concerning to me. Netflix trades at the same Price/Sales as Facebook yet has significantly worse margins and cash flow. These two companies also have similar revenue growth rates, so there is comparability. I could say the same for Google. Each dollar of Netflix's lower margin revenue being valued at twice that of Google's is scary.
Enterprise Value, Forward P/E, PEG Ratio, and Price/Sales provided by Yahoo Finance Wall Street's Opinion
Wall Street's consensus price target is $331.12, which represents about 5% downside potential. With that being said, analyst opinions are all over the map. Many remain bullish and some have begun to buck the trend. My opinion aligns with that of Scott Devit of Stifel, which downgraded the stock a few months ago and gave the following comment:
We are attracted to Netflix's business and competitive position but believe share price may have sprinted ahead of fundamentals in the short-term.
We believe share price outperformance over the next several quarters may be more difficult to achieve given the recent run and increasing expectations."
2. Netflix's Financing Strategy One thing I fundamentally disagree with is how Netflix is financing its content production costs. Netflix has increasingly turned to the debt markets. This poses a number of real risks:
Interest rates are now increasing, which will increase Netflix's cost basis. Netflix is a long way from producing positive free cash flow. Proceeds from new debt offerings are actually used to help pay for financing costs, which I hate to see. I don't think debt should be used so willingly unless it can be supported by a company's operations. Even though Netflix credit rating improved earlier this year, its debt offerings are still considered junk bonds . That's an ominous sign and investors should pay more attention to credit rating agencies given they have a more realistic view of a given company's performance and outlook.
Keep in mind that Netflix has a great opportunity to raise capital in the secondary markets right now. This would be dilutive to existing shareholders, but not really that much. Raising $10 billion in equity for a company that has an enterprise value of $147.5 billion would dilute shareholders less than 10%. Netflix won't be doing this anytime soon and gave the following comments in its latest earnings release :
We have about $2.6 billion in cash and we will continue to raise debt as needed to fund our increase in original content. Our debt levels are quite modest as a percentage of our enterprise value, and we believe the debt is lower cost of capital compared to equity."
Netflix is certainly right in terms of its debt vs. enterprise value. However, that's just one viewpoint and there's many others that don't look as good. As I've already pointed out, Netflix can't support any debt based on free cash flow. Revenue vs. debt is high and so is net income vs. debt. Lets not forget that during a correction or recession, Netflix could see a major drop in enterprise value and the statement above might not appear so accurate anymore. Looking for the cheapest form of capital isn't always the best pathway, risk needs to be a major factor as well. At the very least, a combination of equity and debt would seem like a more reasonable strategy.
3. Competitive Environment Bullish Netflix investors often point to the company's ability to raise prices as rationale for the lofty valuation. While I still consider Netflix a good value at $10.99/month and think prices will be able to continue slowly increasing, there is definitely a ceiling to this. The competitive environment is getting more crowded and there's now many options for consumers:
HBO Now - $14.99/month Amazon Prime Video - comes with annual $119 Prime Membership Hulu - $7.99/month Sling TV - $20/month for 30+ channels Philo - 37 channels at $16/month or 46 channels at $20/month AT&T will be debuting its own $15/month low-cost subscription bundle in the future. At current prices, Netflix has had the luxury of very low customer churn. Keep in mind that as prices increase, so will customer churn, which will likely lead to slowing subscriber growth, slowing revenue growth, and increasing customer acquisition costs.
Netflix investors also need to be cautious about other tech giants entering the market like Apple ( AAPL ), Google, and Facebook. I'd be especially fearful of Google and Facebook entering the space given they both have huge existing user-bases and nearly unlimited capital at their disposal.
Conclusion With 125 million subscribers, Netflix has an unrivaled membership base, which has translated to impressive revenue growth. With that being said, I believe the stock's valuation has been pushed to unsustainable levels. Netflix's Price/Sales ratio of 12x is unrealistic for a company that has gross margins below 50%. There's other stocks with a similar growth rate, strong free cash flow, and far less downside risk compared to Netflix. Increasing leverage and the competitive environment are also major concerns of mine. Netflix is a company that I like, but I will wait until the stock trades at a much lower valuation before I open up a position.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, FB.
